Science Programs The DOE Office of Science sponsors basic research at over 300 institutions across the country, including universities, national laboratories, nonprofits, and private sector institutions. Funding is awarded on a competitive basis using peer review. Research efforts range from single-investigator grants to large team-based projects. We administer research through eight program offices, spanning a broad range of disciplines: Accelerator R&D and Production , Advanced Scientific Computing Research , Basic Energy Sciences , Biological and Environmental Research , Fusion Energy Sciences , High Energy and Nuclear Physics , and Isotope R&D and Production . The DOE Office of Science Early Career Research Program provides annual funding opportunities for outstanding early career scientists in the disciplines supported by the DOE Office of Science. In addition, our Office of Workforce Development for Teachers and Scientists sponsors student internships and other education and training programs at DOE’s 17 national laboratories. If the right evidence is present, forensic science can help investigators solve crimes, including cases that have long been cold. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Scientific Research Make world-class discoveries National Conservation Lands comprise a natural scientific laboratory that attracts scientists from around the world. The scientific values found within many National Conservation Lands units open the door to valuable research on topics ranging from geology, paleontology, archaeology and history to biology, botany and ecosystem studies. Researchers are discovering new species of dinosaurs, studying best practices for rangeland management, determining butterfly diversity, reintroducing endangered species, examining the dynamics of riparian areas, and much more on these lands. Many research projects on the National Conservation Lands are conducted through partnerships with scientists and scientific organizations including universities, government agencies, American Indian tribes, special-focus groups and non-governmental organizations. Scientific projects inform the decision-making process of BLM managers. Close working relationships between scientists and BLM managers and staff lead to mutually beneficial outcomes. As part of their effort to map protein networks associated with autism, researchers also tried to better understand some of these interactions with brain organoid experiments in the lab. Courtesy of the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at the University of California, San Francisco. By Rachel Fairbank Published September 1, 2026 Scientists have mapped a network of interacting proteins, to create a “blueprint” of some of the molecular changes that are associated with autism spectrum disorder. The developmental disability affects an estimated 1 out of every 31 people in the U.S., runs in families, and is highly heritable , suggesting a genetic component. However, the underlying biology is highly complex. Hundreds of variations in genes and the proteins they produce may be involved in autism. The new map is the largest of its kind and tracks over 1800 proteins that may play molecular roles in the condition. “Autism may have hundreds of different genetic starting points, but this study suggests that many of those different roads converge on the same molecular intersections,” says Christian Schaaf , a genetics researcher at the University of Heidelberg, who was not involved in the work. However, in the process, it violates certain “selection rules” imposed by parity and rotational symmetry, both fundamental physics concepts. Scientists thought one of these types of forbidden beta decays was completely blocked in certain circumstances. Researchers found a previously undiscovered species of titanosaur (illustrated above) among other fossilized creatures at the site. Illustration by Gabriel Lio By Meghie Rodrigues Published March 5, 2025 In Northern Patagonia, paleontologists have unearthed an ancient lagoon ecosystem surrounded by sand dunes and palm trees where prehistoric creatures thrived. Excavations of 78 million year-old rocks, from a quarry just outside General Roca city in Argentina, yielded a treasure trove of 432 fossils belonging to over a hundred animal groups. The majority of the fossils belonged to turtles, but other residents were fish, crocodile relatives, slugs—including the first fossil record of the Neocyclotidae , a family of tropical land snails, and the first record of Leptinaria , a genus of small tropical air-breathing land snails—and dinosaurs . pages.text: Scientists found 20 Homo naledi in a cave. Why are they all female? | National Geographic HISTORY & CULTURE Scientists found 20 ancient hominins in a cave, and a mystery: Why are they all female? A new protein analysis of Homo naledi skeletons reveals a curious twist—none of them seem to have Y chromosomes. Researchers have excavated hundreds of Homo naledi bones from the cave system known as Rising Star, including around 150 teeth, which can be used to determine the sex of skeletons. They now suspect that the majority of the individuals at the site were biologically female. By Helen Thompson Photographs by Robbie Shone Published June 24, 2026 Around 300,000 years ago, a cave in South Africa became the final resting place of at least 20 human cousins from the ancient species Homo naledi . Today, researchers have determined that all of those individuals appear to be missing a Y chromosome—the telltale genetic marker for males—and are likely female. Using a new method for sampling ancient teeth, the team was able to collect chemical clues about the sex of each skeleton without destroying it. The technique has the potential to “transform paleontology for several decades,” says Lee Berger , who is the National Geographic Society's Explorer in Residence, paleoanthropologist at Wits University in South Africa, and a co-author on the new study. Berger and his colleagues first discovered Homo naledi ’s bones in the cave system called Rising Star in 2013. It can then transmit information about the digestive tract to a reader outside the body. MIT News Ingestible sensors provide a helpful way to monitor a person’s health from the inside. But finding effective ways to power them has been a challenge. They typically use either standard batteries, which contain harmful chemicals, or external sources that provide energy wirelessly. Now, scientists have created digestible, paper-based batteries that can power medical devices inside the body and eventually get broken down. The technology, described in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering on September 21, has so far been tested only in pigs. If further studies confirm its safety in humans, it could one day power all sorts of medical devices. “For many of the systems we’re developing, we need power, and we power the system through different ways,” says study co-author Giovanni Traverso , a mechanical engineer at MIT and gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, in a statement . “Often, we use batteries, so the question here was: Could we develop a battery that was bioresorbable, and then apply that across a range of application areas?” Bioresorbable Batteries for Transient Ingestible Bioelectronics Watch on The battery contains electrodes made with the metals magnesium and molybdenum, which are safe for human consumption in small amounts. Researchers have identified a cluster of sleep-related traits linked to more severe depression, offering new insights into how the body's internal clock may influence mental health and treatment. But what if these sleep habits were more than symptoms of the illness? Researchers in Australia suggest they could be signs of a distinct form of depression. The idea that a misfiring body clock might do more harm than cause a bad night’s sleep isn’t new. But a study in the British Journal of Psychiatry proposes that people with this cluster of traits may have circadian depression— a potential subtype in which a disrupted body clock is a core feature. pages.text: Scientists may have solved the mystery of Nanotyrannus | National Geographic SCIENCE Teen T. rex or totally different dinosaur? The debate over Nanotyrannus gets a new twist. After decades of fierce debate, researchers say fossils once thought to be juvenile T. rex actually belong to a separate, sleeker species of tyrannosaur. Nanotyrannus was long thought to be the very prey it's shown attacking in the illustration above, a young Tyrannosaurus rex . New evidence suggests it was a different class of dinosaur. Anthony Hutchings By Nicholas St. Fleur Published October 30, 2025 One of paleontology’s most polarizing problems is a teenage Tyrannosaurus rex with an identity crisis, and two scientists say they’ve solved it. In 1942, researchers from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History found the skull of a small theropod in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. After scientists classified it as the new species Nanotyrannus lancensis in 1988, the skull sparked four decades of fierce debate: Do such fossils of small and slender tyrannosaurs represent a teenage version of the fearsome T. rex , or an entirely distinct dinosaur? Now, after analyzing more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the authors of a new study have declared that Nanotyrannus was a swift and lean dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex in the twilight of the tyrant’s reign. The top images was created from visible spectrum photographs and the bottom from near infrared photography. Image Courtesy M Vavulin, Antiquity Publications Ltd By Annie Roth Published July 30, 2025 From tribal symbols to the name of an ex, people have long adorned their skin with ink. Countless cultures have developed and practiced the art of tattooing for at least 5,000 years. Among the most famous examples are Ötzi the Iceman, found frozen in the Alps with 61 tattoos , and the Chinchorro mummy of ancient Chile, marked with black, mustache-like dots thought to be tattoos beneath his nose. Despite their ubiquity, ancient tattoos are difficult to study. Scientists have relied on inked-up mummies for glimpses into the early origins of the art form. But tattoos on their skin are often faded or rendered invisible by the mummification process, limiting how much researchers can glean from them. Now, new technologies are helping bring these ancient tattoos back to life. pages.text: Scotland and Netherlands share series after third ODI rained off - BBC Sport Image source, Cricket Scotland Image caption, There was no play under the shadow of the Wallace Monument Published 1 September 2026 Scotland and the Netherlands have tied their one-day-international series 1-1 after the third match was abandoned without a ball being bowled at Stirling County following heavy and persistent rain throughout the day. The series was arranged at short notice as the Dutch women sought to regain their ODI ranking and avoid a substantial funding cut next year. The visitors won the opening match by 58 runs at Clydesdale, with the Scots securing a convincing nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected second in Stirling. However, it does mean that the Dutch have done enough to secure their ranking and much-needed funds. pages.description: Scotland hold on for a nervy nine-run victory over Canada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense tri-series match in Forfarshire.
pages.text: Scotland beat Canada by nine runs to reach World Cup Qualifier - BBC Sport Image source, Ian Jacobs Image caption, Fin McCreath was Scotland's top scorer with 112 Published 7 August 2026 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 tri-series, Forthill Scotland 281-7 (50 overs): McCreath 112; Shirzad 3-55 Canada 272 (49.2): Samra 78; McMullen 3-43 Scotland won by nine runs Scorecard Scotland held on for a nervy nine-run victory over Canada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 match in Forfarshire. Fin McCreath's 112, his first international century, helped the hosts post 281-7 at Forthill. Canada hit 50 inside eight overs thanks to Yuvraj Sumra (78), but they fell to 181-7 only for a partnership of 84 by Ansh Patel and captain Saad Bin Zafar to take them close to their target before George Munsey's catch secured Scotland's win with four balls remaining. Scotland are now assured a place at next year's Qualifier as Canada cannot catch them in the League 2 standings. It was the first game of the tri-series, which also involves the United Arab Emirates, to beat the wet weather after two washouts. Grange batter McCreath reached his century from 135 balls in the 47th over. pages.title: Scotland beat Netherlands by nine wickets to level ODI series - BBC Sport
pages.description: Scotland level their one-day international series with the Netherlands at 1-1 after a thumping nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected match in Stirling.
pages.text: Scotland beat Netherlands by nine wickets to level ODI series - BBC Sport Image source, Cricket Scotland Image caption, Scotland made short work of chasing down the Dutch total after a wet morning in Stirling Published 31 August 2026 Second one-day international, Stirling Netherlands 129-9 (32 overs): De Leede 58; Maqsood 3-20, Carter 2-18 Scotland 130-1 (16.2 overs): S Bryce 70*, Carter 33* Scotland won by nine wickets Scorecard Scotland levelled their one-day international series with the Netherlands at 1-1 after a thumping nine-wicket victory in a rain-affected match in Stirling. Sarah Bryce, captaining the side in the absence of her sister Kathyrn, led the way with an unbeaten 70 as the hosts chased down their target of 130 in just over half of their allotted 32 overs, in a game which was originally scheduled for Sunday but fell foul of the weather. The Dutch had enjoyed a 58-run win in Glasgow on Friday and this was another one-sided contest. Darcy Carter made an early breakthrough, taking the wickets of Netherlands openers Phebe Molkenboer and Sanya Khurana, who had piled on more than 150 in last week's encounter. Abtaha Maqsood also took two quick wickets to leave the visitors reeling on 39-4. Maqsood struck again but Babette de Leede made 58 before being run out, while Caroline de Lange added 20 on the way to their total of 129-9. Scotland lost Maryam Faisal after four balls but Carter (33 not out) and Bryce made sure of a comprehensive success. pages.title: Scotland coast to win over Ireland as both reach Super Six phase - BBC Sport
pages.description: Scotland's bowlers make short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progress to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai.
pages.text: Scotland coast to win over Ireland as both reach Super Six phase - BBC Sport Image source, ICC/Getty Images Image caption, Kirstie Gordon took four wickets for just four runs in Dubai Published 18 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Ireland 71 (19.3 overs): Lewis 20; Gordon 4-4, Maqsood 3-15 Scotland 72-2 (8.3 overs): Carter 30, Fraser 21 Scotland win by eight wickets Scotland's bowlers made short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progressed to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai. Kirstie Gordon ripped through the Irish top order, the left-arm spinner taking four wickets for just four runs. Abtaha Maqsood claimed three wickets, Kathryn Bryce struck twice and Priyanaz Chatterji picked up her 50th T20 International wicket as Ireland were dismissed for just 71. Captain Gaby Lewis top scored for Ireland on 20, with Georgina Dempsey (12), Abbi Harrison (11) and Jane Maguire (11*) the others to reach double figures. In reply, Darcey Carter (30) and Katherine Fraser (21) enjoyed a 53-run opening partnership, with Kathryn Bryce (7*) and Sarah Bryce (4*) steering Scotland home in the ninth over. Scotland finished second behind unbeaten Sri Lanka in Group A, with Ireland in third place. Netherlands and Pakistan are guaranteed passage from Group B as Zimbabwe and Bangladesh vie for the remaining spot. pages.description: The BBC agrees an exclusive deal to broadcast live all Scotland men's international football matches in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.
pages.text: Scotland men's internationals to be shown live on BBC - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Live coverage of Steve Clarke's Scotland starts with a visit to Greece Published 7 March 2025 The BBC has agreed an exclusive contract to broadcast live all Scotland men's international football matches in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup. It is part of a wider deal agreed with European governing body Uefa that also includes matches involving Northern Ireland and Wales - the first time the broadcaster has secured live rights for all three of the UK's devolved nations. The contract includes all 14 live Scotland matches, beginning with the first leg of the Nations League play-off in Greece on 20 March and including June friendlies against Iceland and Leichtenstein as well as World Cup qualifiers. Director BBC Scotland Hayley Valentine said: "I'm so excited that millions of Scotland fans will now be able to enjoy free-to-air access to all Scotland's international matches. pages.title: Scotland propose Titwood venue for 2030 T20 World Cup - BBC Sport
pages.description: Glasgow's Titwood has been chosen as the proposed Scottish venue for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2030.
pages.text: Scotland propose Titwood venue for 2030 T20 World Cup - BBC Sport Image source, SNS Image caption, Titwood has been the home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876 Published 11 November 2026 Glasgow's Titwood has been chosen as the proposed Scottish venue for the ICC Men's T20 World Cup in 2030. Home of Clydesdale Cricket Club since 1876, the ground is in the Pollokshields area of the city. The board of Cricket Scotland say their decision came following "engagement and consultation with the ICC, ECB and other strategic partners". The 2030 World Cup is being co-hosted by England & Wales, Scotland and Ireland. It will be the first major tournament in Scotland since the 1999 Cricket World Cup when The Grange in Edinburgh staged two group matches. Titwood would require a major overhaul and the next steps include talks with the Scottish and UK governments. Scotland's women met the Netherlands in a one-day international at Titwood in August, while the men played six T20 internationals there in June 2025. pages.title: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport
pages.description: Scotland women succumb to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy Group A fixture.
pages.text: Scotland women beaten by Sri Lanka in second Emerging Trophy group fixture - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Published 13 November 2026 ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy Scotland 111-8 (20 overs): Carter 62; Masqood 3-18 Sri Lanka 115-6 (18.1 overs): Gunaratne 49; Kumari 2-15, Sandeepani 2-18 Sri Lanka win by four wickets Scotland succumbed to a four-wicket defeat by Sri Lanka in their second Emerging Nations Trophy campaign Group A fixture. Having opened with victory over Papua New Guinea, the Scots batted first against Sri Lanka but were restricted to 111-8 in Ajman, United Arab Emirates. Darcey Carter top scored on 62 runs off 55 deliveries while Sathya Sandeepani and Sugandika Kumari took two wickets each. Sri Lanka's Vishmi Gunaratne amassed 49 runs off 41 deliveries, with captain Harshitha Samarawickrama contributing 24. Abatha Masqood took three wickets, becoming the Scots' top wicket taker in WT20Is, her 77 surpassing current captain Kathryn Bryce. Ten nations are participating in the UAE, split into two groups of five before a Super Six stage to determine the final on 25 November. Scotland play the hosts next, with UAE having opened with defeat by Ireland, who picked up a first win. Twelve years on from his debut - off the bench in a Poland friendly - he surpassed his friend and fellow Liverpool legend, Kenny Dalglish, whose record haul had stood for 40 years. After moving level with the man they - and he - will always call King, the Tottenham Hotspur left-back shifted chat towards the former forward, his commendable humility laid bare. But, in St Gallen, the spotlight shone on one of Scotland's favourite sons as he moves solo at the summit, even if the scoreline was a disappointment. Scott Milliren Scott Milliren is the Director of the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) within the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI). In this role, he oversees a multi-billion-dollar portfolio dedicated to advancing the commercial deployment and scaling of innovative energy, materials, and industrial manufacturing technologies. His leadership supports CMEI’s mission to secure stable domestic supply chains, strengthen American manufacturing, and steward federal resources to provide affordable, reliable, and secure energy for the nation. Before joining OCED, Milliren served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, where he provided strategic guidance on organizational transformation and team development, implementing executive orders aimed at modernizing the commission. Milliren’s career spans more than three decades in the oil and gas services industry, working in both public and private sectors across all segments of energy production, including drilling, equipment manufacturing, production, and completion. Scott Pappano Scott Pappano Scott Pappano currently serves as the Principal Deputy Administrator of the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA). Mr. Pappano has dedicated nearly 35 years of service to the United States Navy as a submarine officer and acquisition leader, including at the rank of Vice Admiral before retiring in May 2025. Throughout his career, Mr. Pappano not only commanded at sea, but shaped the future of undersea warfare and strategic deterrence for generations to come. Pappano served onboard five submarines, including command of USS Buffalo (SSN 715) while forward deployed in Guam. Assignments ashore included submarine tactics development, Navy nuclear power training, defense international security policy, and Navy programming. After selection as an acquisition professional, Pappano served as Major Program Manager for the Strategic and Attack Submarine Program Office (PMS 392). As a flag officer, Mr. Pappano served in some of the Navy’s most critical leadership roles, including Director of the Comprehensive Test Facility, Commander of the Naval Undersea Warfare Center, Program Executive Officer for Strategic Submarines, and Assistant Secretary of the Navy (Research, Development and Acquisition). pages.description: The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout in the UK have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle.
pages.text: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Games currently cannot be shown live between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 29 October 2026 The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle. The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season. BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon. The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes. Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time. While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday. Other leagues now tend to stagger kick-off times so the top divisions do not all play at the same time, meaning the blackout could not be applied. In the UK, 3pm remains the traditional, default kick-off time for all leagues from the very top down through non-league. SCIENCE LAELAPS Scrappy Fossils Yield Possible Dinosaur Blood Cells By Riley Black Published June 16, 2015 • 8 min read Last week, a little movie called Jurassic World debuted. You might have heard something about it . Paleontologists certainly have been jawing about it for a while, particularly how the movie’s dinosaurs stack up against the actual animals emerging from the rock.* But all the arguments about enfluffled dinosaurs and bunny hands have missed a more fundamental issue – could scientists ever recover enough intact dinosaur goo to populate a real Jurassic World? When the first Jurassic Park premiered in 1993, finding non-avian dinosaur DNA seemed a certainty. Two days before the official release of the movie Raúl Cano and colleagues announced that they had sequenced the DNA of a 135-120 million year old, amber-encased weevil. Woodward and colleagues announced that they had sequenced DNA from an 80 million year old dinosaur bone fragment. It seemed that life had found a way. Screening for Type 1 Diabetes Apr. 17, 2026 Key points Type 1 diabetes develops in stages and may start a long time before a person needs insulin. People at high risk for type 1 diabetes can benefit from screening before symptoms appear. Knowing they’re in the early stages of type 1 diabetes can help people notice symptoms and avoid serious complications. Who should be offered screening? People with a family member who has type 1 diabetes are 15 times more likely to develop type 1 than the general population and should be offered screening. It’s important to note, though, that most people who develop type 1 don’t have a family member with the condition. Screening can begin at 2 years old. Why get screened? Type 1 diabetes is often an emergency diagnosis. A person likely doesn't know they have type 1 diabetes until a serious complication happens, such as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). pages.title: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic
pages.description: These reptiles have roamed the oceans for 100 million years. We've put them at risk, but with a little help, they're rebounding.
pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. The West Pacific population has fewer than a thousand females. A flatback sea turtle kicks up sand while digging a nest on Crab Island, off Australia’s northeast coast. Prior to that, he obtained both Bachelor's and Master's degrees in Aerospace Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. SearchGov makes it easier for people to find the information they need from federal websites. As the search engine used by thousands of federal websites, SearchGov supports more than 200 million searches a year. SearchGov shares its history with USA.gov , beginning when internet entrepreneur Eric Brewer donated a powerful search engine to the government. In 2000, USA.gov, at the time named FirstGov.gov, debuted. It featured a search box that allowed users to search across government websites. In 2010, SearchGov expanded to serve agencies throughout the U.S. government. Learn how SearchGov helps agencies connect with the people they serve. Searching for a Job with a Mental Health Condition Written by Coursera Staff • Updated on Nov 29, 2023 Get tips on how to navigate your job search with a mental health condition. Job searches are stressful for almost everyone, however, for those struggling with mental health conditions, looking for a job can feel particularly overwhelming. According to Forbes Media, one in five employees has a diagnosable mental health condition [ 1 ]. You are not alone. In this article, we'll cover some things to consider during your job search, as well as tips for alleviating some of the stress that can come with applying to a new role. The application process Before you start applying for jobs, consider your personal goals and the kind of career you want. How would a particular position fit in with your long term mental health needs? Your mental (and physical) health should be your first priority. Learn if you are eligible for a voucher and how to apply. What are Section 8 housing choice vouchers? The Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) Program, also called Section 8, is run by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The program gives you a voucher to help you afford safe, private housing. Your local public housing agency (PHA) manages Section 8 vouchers. How Section 8 housing vouchers work Specific groups may qualify to use Section 8 vouchers to find housing, including: Families with a low income Seniors People with disabilities Here is what to expect from the program: You can choose any housing that meets the program requirements, such as a single-family home, townhouse, or apartment. Housing choice vouchers can pay for all or part of your rent. The PHA pays its part of the rent to the owner (landlord), and you as the tenant pay the difference. pages.text: Secure Transfer, Restricted-Use Data Lake (STRUDL) | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Secure Transfer, Restricted-Use Data Lake (STRUDL) More in This Section Close Chief Evaluation Office (CEO) About CEO CEO Library Resources Topic Areas Public Use Data Lake (PUDL) Secure Transfer, Restricted-Use Data Lake (STRUDL) Engaging with STRUDL STRUDL - How to Apply STRUDL FAQs STRUDL Forms DOL's Clearinghouse (CLEAR) Events Academic Engagement U.S. Department of Labor’s (DOL) Secure Transfer, Restricted-Use Data Lake (STRUDL) provides authorized external and internal researchers secure access to confidential data. The program aims to support approved social science research projects that align with DOL’s mission. In summary, the STRUDL allows researchers to address important research questions of interest to the academic community, the general public, and DOL. These data have already been paid for by the public and are being reutilized rather than discarded. Storing and carefully reusing them ensures good stewardship. Approved researchers, those who submit a successful STRUDL application, can access, link, and utilize restricted-use microdata from a variety of DOL sources. Prior to public release, staff from DOL’s disclosure review process will review the analyses and statistics on DOL data. Subject matter experts (SMEs) review the paper for factual accuracy only. SMEs do not review authors’ tone, framing, or conclusions. Once cleared, researchers can publish their results in reports and other professional outlets.
